lead: A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) can move to many possible next states on the same input symbol. It exists to give a compact description of regular languages. It is used when a regular expression is easier to translate into parallel choices, such as pattern matching in text editors or validating a UPI ID.

blocks.text: An NFA is a 5‑tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) where Q is a finite set of states, Σ is a finite input alphabet, δ : Q × Σ → 2^Q is the transition function, q₀ ∈ Q is the start state, and F ⊆ Q is the set of accept states.
For a state p and symbol a, δ(p, a) returns the set of states reachable from p on input a. The set may be empty, contain one state, or contain many states.

blocks.where: δ̂ is the extended transition function; w = w₁…w_k is a string; δ̂(q, ε) = {q}.

blocks.text: A string w is accepted if at least one state in δ̂(q₀, w) belongs to F. Only one accepting computation path is required.
Nondeterminism lets the automaton guess a position in the input where a pattern starts. The guess is represented by branching to several states.
If any branch reaches an accept state, the whole NFA accepts. The examiner often expects you to argue that the existence of a successful branch is enough.

items: Branching reduces the number of states compared with an equivalent DFA.
Designing an NFA from a regular expression follows a systematic construction.
Later we will remove the branching by subset construction.

blocks.text: Construct an NFA that accepts any binary string containing the substring 101. Use states p (start), q (seen 1), r (seen 10), and s (accept).

items: From p on 1 go to q. On 0 stay in p.
From q on 0 go to r. On 1 stay in q.
From r on 1 go to s. On 0 return to p.
State s has a self‑loop on both 0 and 1.

blocks.text: For input 110101 the NFA follows a single path p → q → q → r → s → s and reaches the accept state s, so the string is accepted.

examples.question: Construct an NFA for the language of all strings over Σ={0,1} that contain the substring 101. Show the computation tree for input 110101 and state whether the input is accepted.
steps: Create states p (start), q (seen 1), r (seen 10), s (accept).
Add transitions as described in the steps block of the section.
Draw the computation tree: root state set {p} after reading nothing.
Since s ∈ accept set, the input is accepted.
examples.answer: The input 110101 is accepted because one computation path reaches the accept state s.

traps: Assuming every possible nondeterministic branch must end in an accept state; only one accepting branch is enough.
Confusing the transition function δ (which returns a set) with a deterministic function that returns a single state.
Treating ε‑moves as ordinary symbols; ε‑moves are handled in the next chapter.
Counting the start state twice when it also appears in the accept set; the start state is counted once.

quiz.q: What are the five components of an NFA?
quiz.a: Q (states), Σ (alphabet), δ (transition function), q₀ (start state), F (accept states).

quiz.q: Explain why an NFA can have fewer states than an equivalent DFA for the same language.
quiz.a: Nondeterminism allows one state to represent several possible histories. The DFA must split these histories into separate states, increasing the count.
After 0: {p,q}. After 1: from p → {p}, from q → {q}. Resulting set = {p,q}.

quiz.q: Design an NFA that accepts strings ending with the suffix 11 over Σ={0,1}. State the start and accept states.
quiz.a: States: s (start), a (seen first 1), f (accept). Transitions: s --0/1--> s; s --1--> a; a --1--> f; a --0--> s; f --0/1--> f. Accept state = f.

quiz.q: A student claims that the NFA shown in the figure accepts the string 001 because both branches from p lead to accept states after reading the third symbol. Identify the mistake.
quiz.a: The figure has no accept states; even if a branch reaches a state, it must be in the accept set F. Moreover, acceptance requires at least one branch to end in F after the whole input, not after a prefix.

quiz.q: What does the notation δ(p, a) = {q₁, q₂} mean in an NFA?
quiz.a: From state p on input symbol a the automaton may move to either q₁ or q₂.

quiz.q: Why is the extended transition function δ̂ defined using a union over intermediate states?
quiz.a: Because at each step the automaton may be in many states simultaneously; the union collects all possible next states.

quiz.q: Using the NFA for substring 101, show the set of active states after reading the prefix 110.
quiz.a: After first 1: {q}. After second 1: {q}. After third 0: {r}. So the active set is {r}.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, NFAs underlie lexical analyzers that scan source code for tokens. Research explores symbolic NFAs that operate on character classes to reduce memory. Cloud‑based firewalls use NFAs to match packet payloads against attack signatures. The next step is to study ε‑moves, which allow spontaneous state changes without consuming input. After that, learn how to convert any NFA to an equivalent DFA using the subset construction.
